A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TSR-SUITE and TimeOmni-1 work. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original ID/OOD evaluations, training ablations, general-reasoning benchmark results and appendix analyses, including Tables 1–4 and Figures 4–9.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds prompt robustness, encoding comparisons, reward sensitivity, training dynamics, data scaling and external benchmark results.

M1.justification: The proposed hierarchical annotation pipeline, supervised fine-tuning followed by GRPO, joint training and task-grounded rewards remain unchanged. Appendix F newly explains text serialization and evaluates an embedding-based comparator; it does not replace the proposed method.

E1.justification: Appendix K adds MTBench, TimeSeriesExam and CaTS-Bench, covering 13 tasks and 3,406 samples. These extend evaluation to financial/weather QA, synthetic anomaly/noise/pattern/similarity questions, retrieval and amplitude/mean comparisons. The original TSR-SUITE coverage remains intact.

E2.justification: The original Table 1 comparators are retained. Appendix F.3 adds a newly trained ChatTS-style embedding comparator with a matched Qwen2.5-Instruct-14B backbone. Tables 10–12 additionally compare against source-reported GPT-4o, Phi-3.5 and LLaVA v1.6 Mistral scores; these are identified as published reference results, not fresh baseline runs.

E3.justification: Original evaluation settings are retained, while new experiments introduce matched 14B encoding comparisons, a 100-sample efficiency test, one-epoch reward sweeps and training-data fractions of 25–100%. The no-system-prompt experiment changes answer parsing to handle free-form responses and omits SR, distinguishing its protocol from the original evaluation.

E4.justification: Appendices E.3, F.3, G.1, I and J add substantial analyses of prompt dependence, text versus learned embeddings, reward-component sensitivity, RL optimization dynamics and training-data scaling. These supplement the retained training-stage, joint-training and case-study analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random-seed specifications, confidence intervals or formal significance tests for the reported comparisons. The new training curves and sensitivity sweeps do not introduce statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Original Tables 1–2 and the retained appendix results are numerically unchanged. v2 adds extensive robustness, encoding, efficiency, scaling and external benchmark results. In Tables 10–12, newly reported TimeOmni-1/base-model averages are respectively 58.1/49.2, 47.8/46.9 and 63.5/65.0, showing mixed external transfer rather than uniform gains.

T1.justification: The reasoning formulation, context-sufficiency principle, SFT/GRPO objectives and reward definitions in Equations 1–9 remain unchanged. Appendix K repeats the existing probabilistic formulation; no new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same substantive contributions: the four-task reasoning suite, unified two-stage model, joint-training benefits and headline GPT-4.1 comparisons. The added resource-availability statement does not redefine the scientific claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations linking prompt robustness to internalized priors, reward design to training stability, and external transfer to contextual alignment. Appendix F.3 newly qualifies text serialization as suitable for modest sequence lengths and dimensionality, while discussing encoder data requirements and possible advantages for longer or higher-dimensional inputs. Appendix J adds interpretations of data scaling.

D1.justification: v1 already supplied detailed prompts and training configurations. v2 adds explicit public code/checkpoint availability statements and access links, sequence-length and tokenizer-budget statistics, serialization details, and the response cap used for training-dynamics evaluation. These materially expand reproducibility documentation without establishing a change to the original training configuration.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations including ChatTime, ITFormer, OpenTSLM, ViT and the three external benchmarks, and discusses serialization relative to encoder-based approaches. The broader distinction between time-series language and reasoning models, and the paper's central novelty positioning, remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative structure are retained. Changes include localized related-work wording, the conference header, ethics and reproducibility statements, an LLM-use appendix, and additional appendix subsections. Existing appendices are renumbered with limited reordering.

P2.justification: v2 adds eight tables covering input statistics, prompt robustness, encoding/efficiency and external benchmarks, plus Figures 11–14 for sensitivity, dynamics and scaling. Existing displays are retained with reflow and renumbering: v1 Table 4 becomes Table 6, and case-study Tables 5–8 become Tables 13–16.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses gaps in v1's validation of robustness, encoding choices and external time-series QA transfer, while adding useful applicability limits and code/checkpoint access information. These gains strengthen the paper beyond merely adding scores. Some new interpretations overreach: Table 12 shows lower CaTS-Bench performance than the base model, and Figures 13–14 contain exceptions to claimed monotonic scaling. Those localized weaknesses temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial improvement in empirical scrutiny and reproducibility.
